svg.text: A cafe claims its cupcakes average 200 cal. Buy one a day for 10 days, weigh the calories, and put the claim on trial. Built in R.

text.tspan: A hunch is not proof, so you collect
then compare ONE sample mean to
ONE fixed value set before the data.

svg.text: Is a sample mean far enough from a fixed
reference to doubt that reference value?
We use the t (not z) because s is estimated from a small sample.
H₀ (null): give the cafe the benefit of the doubt
the true mean is the claim
4 · THE DATA — far from 200, or noise?
Mean x̄ = 214.4 sits above the claim. But
baking is messy: is the 14.4-cal gap big
The mean is on trial — not one unusual cupcake.
s = 20.9 means cupcakes vary a lot. The claim fixes
the center but not the spread, so we estimate spread
from the sample and convert it to a standard error.
7 · THE NULL WORLD — "if true, cupcakes vary around 200"
each dot = one cupcake under the null
8 · STANDARD ERROR — spread of the mean
Individuals vary by s = 20.9, but the
average of 10 is far more stable.
If μ were 200, means of 10 cupcakes would
typically wiggle around 200 by about 6.6 cal.
That 6.6 is our measuring stick for the gap.
9 · ONE CUPCAKE vs THE MEAN OF TEN
10 · THE t-STATISTIC — the gap in SEs
How many standard errors is the gap? That
df = n − 1 = 9. We compare 2.18 to a t-distribution
with 9 degrees of freedom — fatter tails than z,
because s was estimated from only 10 cupcakes.
11 · THE p-VALUE — would |t|≥2.18 happen by chance?
Would happen ~6% of the time if H₀ were true — suspicious, but above 0.05.
13 · VERDICT & MORE DATA — power shrinks the SE
p = 0.0575 > 0.05 → don't reject H₀; the n=10 CI still includes 200.
More data shrinks SE; mean barely moved (213.4) yet now clears 200.
